content: Style question: are there ever benefits to writing refine foo ?_ ?_ (all the holes at the end) versus apply foo? Excepting for elaboration edge cases I find apply more clear, but wasn't sure if I was missing any subtlety.
refine can use the expected type of the expression

About style purely, in such a case where you don't really use refine for something more than apply, I agree apply is a more natural word, but I like that refine indicates the number of subgoals. In the end I don't have a clear preference.

I prefer apply except when I can use dot-notation thanks to the expected type:
refine .bar ?_ > apply Foo.bar
I suspect refine is faster since it doesn't have to guess the number of arguments
Actually, apply is faster because it doesn't have to elaborate the application.

Personally the following doesn't feel like an "elaboration edge case" (so judge for yourself if this is relevant):

refine does result in a different order of the goals, which can be significant... a common case where i chose refine over apply for this reason is when using docs#CategoryTheory.Limits.PullbackCone.IsLimit.mk ; with apply, the proof goals come before specifying the lift goal, which gives you 0 grip on getting to the right value for lift. on the other hand, fapply ... and refine ... ?_ ?_ ?_ gives you the goals such that you specify the lift morphisms before proving the correctness.

more precisely, apply will order the resulting holes in a "dependent first" order, in the hope that unification will allow you to close the holes which are depended on while closing this one. on the other hand, fapply and refine will order them in the order that they occur.

(as a side note, the above was written without self-fact-checking, but should generally line up with reality modulo subtleties i can't recall/am unaware of)
but yea, they order goals differently, which means that when using apply you need to be careful that you don't accidentally unify a goal your current goal is dependent on with the wrong value.
For me, considering situations where using one or the other has the same effect, I tend to prefer refine for readability: I can see clearly how many goals will be generated.

@Edward van de Meent I didn't intend to imply that this decision was an elaboration edge case, just wondering if/when it might be a consideration, like how a refine ... ?_; exact foo can't always be combined.

These responses are helpful, thank you all!

Chris Henson said:

Edward van de Meent I didn't intend to imply that this decision was an elaboration edge case, just wondering if/when it might be a consideration, like how a refine ... ?_; exact foo can't always be combined.

yea, i got that, it's just that i had a hard time deciding if this would be relevant to your question, so i wanted to disclaim it.
I see. No, it was a helpful concrete example, thanks for explaining.

Robin Arnez said:

Actually, apply is faster because it doesn't have to elaborate the application.

Could you elaborate a little bit? In addition to bottom-up type inference, apply uses forallMetaTelescopeReducing to peel off binders and then tries unification in a loop with backtracking, so I think it should be slower than refine. Also there's a special typeclass synthesize mechanism in apply, which seems to be slower than term elaborator's synthesizeSyntheticMVars.

apply has a heuristic for figuring out how many arguments to introduce, and this is reasonably reliable. So the backtracking that can happen in general is not really an issue.

I'm not sure what you mean by a special typeclass synthesis mechanism. In both cases, type class search is called, which should be equally fast/slow.
